readings.title: Home Thoughts
readings.challenge: Follow one long sentence of memory and decide whether the speaker is remembering or imagining.
readings.focus: A sudden certainty, in a noisy city, that something is happening at home this minute.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. The poem remembers boys in a Jamaican village. Wis-wis is a tangled vine; guinea grass is a tall grass grown for cattle; mangoes ripen gold with dark specks.

excerpt.locator: “Home Thoughts,” the whole poem; opens “Oh something just now must be happening there! That suddenly and quiveringly here, Amid…”; closes “…daytime dream, there’s something in it, Oh something’s happening there this very minute!”.

questions.prompt: The poem begins and ends with the same certainty. What is the speaker sure of, and where is he when the feeling strikes?
facilitatorNotes: He is “amid the city’s noises,” far from home, and suddenly feels that “something just now must be happening there.” He never says what; the feeling comes first and the pictures follow. The ending insists it is “no daytime dream.”
evidence: Oh something just now must be happening there!
Amid the city’s noises

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker name Davie, Cyril and Georgie instead of simply saying “my friends”?
facilitatorNotes: Names and exact actions (climbing for mangoes, carrying bananas, diving better than anyone) make the memory physical and personal, as if he can see each boy. The boys are quick, skilled and free, which quietly contrasts with the crowded city around the speaker.
evidence: And Georgie—none could ever dive like him—

questions.prompt: Is the speaker remembering the past or imagining the present? What does his insistence that it is happening “this very minute” reveal?
facilitatorNotes: The scenes may be memories of his own boyhood, but he places them in the present, as if home goes on without him. The insistence shows a homesickness strong enough to feel like being there. Readers may find the ending joyful, painful, or both.
evidence:
This is no daytime dream, there’s something in it,
Oh something’s happening there this very minute!

readings.title: The White City
readings.challenge: Explain a speaker’s surprising claim and test whether the poem approves of the feeling it describes.
readings.focus: A sonnet in which hatred of racial injustice becomes a source of strength.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem; this one turns after its eighth line. When McKay wrote, Black Americans faced segregation and frequent racial violence. A “goaded mass” is a crowd driven like cattle; “wanton” means wild and unrestrained.
readings.contentNote: The speaker declares a lifelong hatred and calls the white world a “hell.” The poem responds to racism in America around 1920.

excerpt.locator: “The White City,” the whole sonnet; opens “I will not toy with it nor bend an inch. Deep in the secret chambers of my heart I muse…”; closes “…tides, the wharves, the dens I contemplate, Are sweet like wanton loves because I hate.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say his hate does for him?
facilitatorNotes: Without it he would be “a skeleton, a shell”; it “feeds” him “vital blood.” He does not hide it or give in to it but bears it “nobly” and in secret. The claim is startling because hate is usually thought to destroy a person, not keep him alive.
evidence: My being would be a skeleton, a shell,
Did not forever feed me vital blood.

questions.prompt: In the last six lines the speaker looks at the city. What does he see, and what does the final line mean?
facilitatorNotes: Trains driving the “goaded mass,” towers, the fortified harbour, wharves and dens, all seen “through a mist.” His hate makes these sights “sweet like wanton loves”: it sharpens his attention and gives the city a fierce, almost thrilling beauty. Readers may find this disturbing or honest, or both.
evidence: I see the mighty city through a mist—
Are sweet like wanton loves because I hate.

questions.prompt: Why is the city called “white”? Does the poem approve of the speaker’s hatred, or only show it?
facilitatorNotes: “White” names the white-ruled world that has made his life a struggle, perhaps also the city’s pale towers in the mist. The speaker is controlled (“I will not toy with it nor bend an inch”) and acts on nothing; his hate is a shield. Some readers will see a defiant strength, others a wound the city has made; the poem lets both stand.
evidence: I will not toy with it nor bend an inch.
And makes my heaven in the white world’s hell

readings.title: I Shall Return
readings.challenge: Track how repetition works in a poem, and notice how one final line changes everything before it.
readings.focus: A promise to return home that ends by revealing a hidden pain.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem; this one ends with a rhymed pair of lines. A fife is a small flute; runes here are old songs. McKay in fact never went back to Jamaica.

excerpt.locator: “I Shall Return,” the whole sonnet; opens “I shall return again; I shall return To laugh and love and watch with wonder-eyes At…”; closes “…runes. I shall return, I shall return again, To ease my mind of long, long years of pain.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker promise to return to? Which senses does each promise use?
facilitatorNotes: Forest fires burning at noon under “sapphire skies” (sight), streams through grass and rushing mountain water, and the fiddle and fife of village dances (sound). He promises to “laugh and love” again, so the return is to a whole way of feeling, not just a place.
evidence: To laugh and love and watch with wonder-eyes

questions.prompt: “I shall return” is repeated again and again. Is it a promise, a prayer or a way of persuading himself?
facilitatorNotes: It could be any of these. Repetition makes the promise firm, but repeating it so often may also suggest doubt, as if the speaker must keep saying it to believe it. Knowing that McKay never went back adds sadness, though the poem itself does not tell us that.
evidence: I shall return, I shall return again,

questions.prompt: How does the last line change the poem?
facilitatorNotes: Until then the sonnet is all pleasure; the final line reveals the reason for returning: “long, long years of pain.” The pain is never explained, so readers must infer it from the distance and the life the speaker lives now. The happy pictures become a cure he longs for.
evidence: To ease my mind of long, long years of pain.

readings.title: On a Primitive Canoe
readings.challenge: Explain a metaphor and a question the speaker himself cannot answer.
readings.focus: An old hand-carved canoe moves the speaker more than the great ship that brought him across the ocean.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. “Primitive” here means made long ago by simple tools, a word of McKay’s time. An adze is a tool for shaping wood. The speaker crossed the Atlantic, as McKay did, to come to America.

excerpt.locator: “On a Primitive Canoe,” the whole sonnet; opens “Here, passing lonely down this quiet lane, Before a mud-splashed window long I pause To…”; closes “…nights and days? I cannot answer but, whate’er it be, An old wine has intoxicated me.”.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker looking at, and where is it?
facilitatorNotes: A canoe behind a “mud-splashed window” in a quiet lane, perhaps in a shop or small museum. It was made “long ago in a dim unknown land” from a single tree, felled with an axe and shaped with an adze. The ordinary, dirty window contrasts with the wonder he feels.
evidence: Before a mud-splashed window long I pause

questions.prompt: What does it mean that the canoe was made “into a symbol of the tender moon”?
facilitatorNotes: Its curved shape resembles a crescent moon. Calling it a “symbol” lifts a hollowed log into art: the maker shaped wood into something that carries meaning and beauty, not only people. “Tender” gives the moon, and the canoe, a gentle feeling.
evidence: Into a symbol of the tender moon.

questions.prompt: Why does the old canoe thrill him more than the “handsome boat” that carried him across the Atlantic? Does he know?
facilitatorNotes: He says he “cannot answer.” The image of “an old wine” suggests that age itself, and a link to remote ancestors and simpler lives, intoxicates him, away from his “harsh life of fretful nights and days.” Readers may connect the canoe to heritage, to childhood, or to the beauty of handmade things.
evidence:
I cannot answer but, whate’er it be,
An old wine has intoxicated me.

readings.title: Winter in the Country
readings.challenge: Follow sentences that run across stanza breaks, and find where the poem turns.
readings.focus: A winter day in the country, the dreary room the speaker must return to, and what he can carry back.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. The speaker is spending a day in the countryside near the sea. A bureau is a chest of drawers; gaslight was lamplight from burning gas, common in poor city rooms.

excerpt.locator: “Winter in the Country,” the whole poem; opens “Sweet life! how lovely to be here And feel the soft sea-laden breeze Strike my flushed…”; closes “…very wind, the winter birds, The glory of the soft sunset, Come there to me in words.”.

questions.prompt: What makes this winter countryside a “paradise” to the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: The sea breeze on his face, the spruce, the bare trees, the sparrow, the “short brown grass asleep,” and a sense of love and peace “beyond my power to express.” Winter is usually bleak in poems, but here even bare branches are “hands” to touch, and everything feels alive and friendly.
evidence: Sweet life! how lovely to be here
Above the short brown grass asleep.

questions.prompt: The fourth stanza turns. Describe the room the speaker must return to. How do the words change?
facilitatorNotes: A “dirty basement room” with a few pieces of furniture, “two crippled chairs,” dust, scars and dim gaslight. The words become harsh and the objects seem injured. The room will “welcome” him, an ironic word for such a place.
evidence:
But oh! to leave this paradise
For the city’s dirty basement room,
Will welcome me....

questions.prompt: “And yet, and yet”: what reaches him even in the basement room, and how?
facilitatorNotes: The wind, the winter birds and the sunset come to him “in words”: through memory and through writing poems like this one. The ending suggests that poetry can carry beauty into an ugly place. Some readers may think words are a poor substitute; the poem’s calm ending suggests the speaker is consoled.
evidence:
This very wind, the winter birds,
The glory of the soft sunset,
Come there to me in words.

readings.title: When Dawn Comes to the City
readings.challenge: Compare two kinds of stanza by their rhythm, sound and repetition.
readings.focus: Dawn in New York against dawn on a remembered island.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. Tenements were crowded city apartment buildings; milk carts delivered milk before sunrise; a lea is a meadow; the rose-apple is a tropical fruit tree. Ned is a donkey and Nannie a goat.

excerpt.locator: “When Dawn Comes to the City,” the whole poem; opens “The tired cars go grumbling by, The moaning, groaning cars, And the old milk carts go…”; closes “…flat rocks joyously! There, oh there! on the island of the sea, There I would be at dawn.”.

questions.prompt: Compare the city stanzas with the island stanzas. How do their lines, sounds and moods differ?
facilitatorNotes: The city stanzas have short, regular lines and heavy words: cars “grumbling,” “moaning, groaning,” workers who “sadly shuffle.” The island stanzas have long lines full of repeated sounds (“crowing, crowing, crowing”) that tumble forward like the stream. The rhythm itself contrasts a tired routine with crowded, joyful life.
evidence:
The tired cars go grumbling by,
The moaning, groaning cars,
Where the cocks are crowing, crowing, crowing,

questions.prompt: The island stanza is repeated word for word, but the city stanza changes. What changes the second time, and why might that matter?
facilitatorNotes: The cars become “crazy, lazy,” the stars are “dying,” a lonely newsboy hums, and “red streaks” announce the dawn. The city moves through time while the island stays exactly the same, fixed in memory. Readers may see the island as a perfect dream or as a place the speaker can no longer change by living in it.
evidence: Under the dying stars.
Red streaks strike through the gray of the sky,

questions.prompt: In New York the speaker sees “dark figures”; on the island he hears “dear old Ned.” What does this difference suggest about what he misses?
facilitatorNotes: The city people are nameless and shadowy, while the island animals are named and loved. He misses belonging among familiar creatures as much as the scenery. Readers might notice the island has no people at all and ask why.
evidence:
Out of the tenements, cold as stone,
Dark figures start for work;
And dear old Ned is braying, braying, braying,

readings.title: The Easter Flower
readings.challenge: Follow a memory that carries both a religious meaning and a private one.
readings.focus: At a cold Easter far from home, the speaker remembers one lily.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. Easter celebrates Christ rising from the tomb. The Easter lily is a white lily that blooms in spring; rime is frost.

excerpt.locator: “The Easter Flower,” the whole poem; opens “Far from this foreign Easter damp and chilly My soul steals to a pear-shaped plot of…”; closes “…And I, a pagan, worshiped at its shrine, Yielding my heart unto its perfumed power.”.

questions.prompt: Where is the speaker, and where does his soul go? Which details mark each place?
facilitatorNotes: He is in a “foreign” place where Easter is “damp and chilly”; his soul goes to “a pear-shaped plot of ground” at home where a lily bloomed. The precise detail of the shape makes the memory vivid and real.
evidence: Far from this foreign Easter damp and chilly
My soul steals to a pear-shaped plot of ground,

questions.prompt: The lily “burst the tomb for freedom sweet and brief.” How does the poem tie the flower to Easter? Why might “freedom” and “brief” matter to this speaker?
facilitatorNotes: Blooming is pictured as rising from the tomb, like the Easter story, so people called it “the resurrection flower.” Its freedom is brief, as a flower’s life is. For someone far from home, “freedom” may also suggest his own longing. Readers can decide how much to read into it.
evidence: It burst the tomb for freedom sweet and brief
And some called it the resurrection flower;

questions.prompt: Others saw “a sacred sign.” How is the speaker’s worship different?
facilitatorNotes: He calls himself “a pagan”: he worships the flower’s beauty and scent, not what it symbolises. He gives his heart to its “perfumed power.” It is a bold self-description in a poem about Easter; some readers will say his real religion is memory and home.
evidence: And many thought it was a sacred sign,
And I, a pagan, worshiped at its shrine, Yielding my heart unto its perfumed power.

readings.title: Alfonso, Dressing to Wait at Table
readings.challenge: Notice how the title and the last stanza change the meaning of a song.
readings.focus: Waiters getting ready for work, and one who sings.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. The speaker is one of a group of waiters. A glory-hole is a cramped storeroom or crew space; rakes are pleasure-loving men; falsetto is a high singing voice; alloy is a cheaper metal mixed into gold. “Wherefore” means why; “importunate” means demanding. “Paleface” was a slang term for a white person.
readings.contentNote: The speaker calls the white diners “palefaces.”

excerpt.locator: “Alfonso, Dressing to Wait at Table,” the whole poem; opens “Alfonso is a handsome bronze-hued lad Of subtly-changing and surprising parts; His moods…”; closes “…ancient places? Soon we shall be beset by clamouring Of hungry and importunate palefaces.”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker describe Alfonso? Find words that show admiration.
facilitatorNotes: He is handsome and “bronze-hued,” his moods are storms, and his voice is gold “without alloy,” pure. The speaker clearly loves to hear him. The admiration makes the last stanza more pointed.
evidence: Alfonso is a handsome bronze-hued lad
Are rarest notes of gold without alloy.

questions.prompt: Who are “we” and “our”? How do the title and the last stanza change what Alfonso’s song means?
facilitatorNotes: They are his fellow waiters, dressing in the crew space. His song of “carefree men” and wine sits against their real evening: serving demanding white customers. The song becomes an escape, a dream of being the one who is served and free.
evidence: Alfonso’s voice of mellow music thrills Our swaying forms
Soon we shall be beset by clamouring Of hungry and importunate palefaces.

questions.prompt: “But, O Alfonso! wherefore do you sing / Dream-songs of carefree men and ancient places?” Is the speaker scolding, pitying or envying Alfonso?
facilitatorNotes: Several readings fit: a gentle warning that reality is about to break in; sadness that such a voice must wait at table; envy or admiration that he can still dream. The question is left unanswered, which lets the reader choose.
evidence: wherefore do you sing Dream-songs of carefree men and ancient places?

readings.title: North and South
readings.challenge: Find the half of the title that the poem never describes.
readings.focus: A sonnet of slow, sunny days in the tropics.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. This poem is a sonnet, fourteen lines long. The “tropic lands” are the warm islands of the Caribbean, such as Jamaica. “Swarthy” means dark-skinned; strands are shores.

excerpt.locator: “North and South,” the whole poem; opens “O sweet are tropic lands for waking dreams! There time and life move lazily along. There…”; closes “…The sea beats softly on the emerald strands— O sweet for quiet dreams are tropic lands!”.

questions.prompt: List the living things in the poem and what each one is doing. What do they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Crickets chirp, lizards loll, children play, a hummingbird darts, a buzzard floats “for endless hours.” Almost everything is relaxed and unhurried; even the buzzard is “leisured.” The poem itself moves “lazily along.”
evidence: Gay-colored lizards loll all through the day,
The leisured buzzard floats upon the breeze,

questions.prompt: The title is “North and South,” but the poem describes only the South. Where is the North?
facilitatorNotes: It is the place the speaker is in now, never named: by implication busy, cold and hurried. Its absence makes the South glow. Readers might also ask whether a picture of “idleness” everywhere is a fair one, or a homesick dream that leaves out work and hardship.
evidence: O sweet are tropic lands for waking dreams!
A breath of idleness is in the air

questions.prompt: The first and last lines are almost the same. What changes, and why frame the poem this way?
facilitatorNotes: “Waking dreams” becomes “quiet dreams,” and the order of the words turns round. The poem circles back on itself, like a daydream returning to its start, and ends more softly than it began.
evidence: O sweet are tropic lands for waking dreams!
O sweet for quiet dreams are tropic lands!

readings.title: The Castaways
readings.challenge: Notice how a poem’s order differs from the order of what the speaker saw.
readings.focus: Spring in a city park, and the people on its benches.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. This poem is a sonnet. A castaway is someone shipwrecked and abandoned; here it means people cast out by society. “Daubed” means smeared with paint.

excerpt.locator: “The Castaways,” the whole poem; opens “The vivid grass with visible delight Springing triumphant from the pregnant earth, The…”; closes “…and deep. Moaning I turned away, for misery I have the strength to bear but not to see.”.

questions.prompt: The first eight lines describe spring. Then: “Not these, not these did I at first behold!” What did he see first? Why does the poem show spring before it?
facilitatorNotes: He first saw the castaways on the benches; the poem reverses that order. The reader enjoys spring and then has it snatched away, so the reader feels the shock the speaker felt.
evidence: Not these, not these did I at first behold!
The castaways of life, a few asleep,

questions.prompt: Compare the words used for spring with the words used for the people. What contrast does the poem draw?
facilitatorNotes: Spring is “triumphant,” “pregnant,” golden, joyful: life renewing itself. The people are “withered,” “desolate,” in shadow. Nature begins again each year; these lives do not.
evidence: Springing triumphant from the pregnant earth,
Some withered women desolate and mean,

questions.prompt: “For misery / I have the strength to bear but not to see.” What does he mean? Is turning away a weakness?
facilitatorNotes: He can endure his own suffering, but watching others suffer is beyond him. It is an honest confession. Readers may call it compassion, since their pain hurts him, or avoidance, since he turns away rather than helping; the poem allows both.
evidence: Moaning I turned away, for misery I have the strength to bear but not to see.

readings.title: Outcast
readings.challenge: Follow a sonnet from longing to loss, and weigh the images it uses for Africa.
readings.focus: A speaker who feels at home neither in the West nor in the land of his ancestors.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. This poem is a sonnet. The “fathers” of the first line are the speaker’s African ancestors. To hold something “in fee” is to own it outright; a clime is a region of the world.
readings.contentNote: The speaker imagines Africa through words such as “jungle” and “darkness,” and speaks of “the white man’s menace.”

excerpt.locator: “Outcast,” the whole poem; opens “For the dim regions whence my fathers came My spirit, bondaged by the body, longs. Words…”; closes “…For I was born, far from my native clime, Under the white man’s menace, out of time.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker long for, and what holds him back?
facilitatorNotes: He longs for “the dim regions whence my fathers came,” but “the great western world holds me in fee”: it owns him, and he bends his knee to its “alien gods.” His spirit is “bondaged,” a word that recalls slavery.
evidence: For the dim regions whence my fathers came My spirit, bondaged by the body, longs.
But the great western world holds me in fee,

questions.prompt: How can he long for words “never heard” and songs that are “forgotten”? What do the words “jungle” and “darkness” add, and do you accept them?
facilitatorNotes: The loss is inherited: whatever his ancestors knew was taken from him before he was born, so he feels it without knowing it. “Jungle” and “darkness” echo Western images of Africa; he may mean them tenderly (“darkness and … peace”), but readers can question whether he has absorbed the very view of Africa the West imposed.
evidence: Words felt, but never heard, my lips would frame;
I would go back to darkness and to peace,

questions.prompt: What does it mean to be born “out of time”? How does the last part of the poem answer the first?
facilitatorNotes: The first eight lines long for return; the last six admit it is impossible. He walks “a ghost,” “a thing apart,” born far from his “native clime” and in the wrong age, under racial threat. “Out of time” can mean in the wrong era, out of rhythm, or too late.
evidence: And I must walk the way of life a ghost Among the sons of earth, a thing apart;
Under the white man’s menace, out of time.

readings.title: Baptism
readings.challenge: Decide what a poem’s central image stands for, and defend your reading.
readings.focus: A speaker who chooses to walk alone into a furnace.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. This poem is a sonnet. Baptism is a ceremony, often with water, marking the start of a new life; this one is by fire. In the Book of Daniel, three young men thrown into a furnace walk out unharmed. “Aspish” means like an asp, a poisonous snake.

excerpt.locator: “Baptism,” the whole poem; opens “Into the furnace let me go alone; Stay you without in terror of the heat. I will go naked…”; closes “…I will come out, back to your world of tears, A stronger soul within a finer frame.”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the speaker call “you,” and what does he ask of them?
facilitatorNotes: Those who fear: they are to stay outside, “in terror of the heat,” while he goes in alone. He separates himself from people who will not face what he will face.
evidence: Into the furnace let me go alone; Stay you without in terror of the heat.

questions.prompt: What does he promise about how he will behave in the fire? What does the fire do in return?
facilitatorNotes: He will not quiver, show defeat or moan. The fire spits spears and its “red aspish tongues shout wordlessly my name,” as if the ordeal were calling him personally. His pride matches the fire’s violence.
evidence: I will not quiver in the frailest bone,
Red aspish tongues shout wordlessly my name.

questions.prompt: What might the furnace stand for? Use the last lines to support your answer.
facilitatorNotes: Any great ordeal: racism, hardship, the struggle of an artist. The fire destroys his fears and remakes him: “A stronger soul within a finer frame.” A “baptism of fire” is a first, testing trial. Readers can defend different readings; the poem names no single meaning.
evidence: Desire destroys, consumes my mortal fears,
A stronger soul within a finer frame.

readings.title: The Lynching
readings.challenge: Read a poem of witness closely, and notice where it places the blame.
readings.focus: A sonnet about a man murdered by a mob and the crowd that comes to look.
readings.context: Claude McKay (1889–1948) grew up in the hills of Jamaica, then a British colony, and came to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) gathers the poems he wrote in America. This poem is a sonnet. A lynching is a murder by a mob, without trial; in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries thousands of Black Americans were lynched, often before crowds. “Char” here means the burned body.
readings.contentNote: This poem describes the burned and hanging body of a man murdered by a mob, and a crowd, including children, that rejoices at it.

excerpt.locator: “The Lynching,” the whole poem; opens “His Spirit in smoke ascended to high heaven. His father, by the cruelest way of pain, Had…”; closes “…little lads, lynchers that were to be, Danced round the dreadful thing in fiendish glee.”.

questions.prompt: The first four lines speak of spirit, heaven, a father and an unforgiven sin. What story do they echo, and why might McKay begin this way?
facilitatorNotes: They echo the death of Christ: a son called back to his Father “by the cruelest way of pain.” The murdered man is given the dignity of a martyr. “The awful sin” is unclear: it may be the crime he was accused of, never tried, or the lynchers’ sin, which remains unforgiven. The poem never says what he was accused of, and that silence matters.
evidence: His Spirit in smoke ascended to high heaven.
His father, by the cruelest way of pain, Had bidden him to his bosom once again;
The awful sin remained still unforgiven.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the star that “Hung pitifully” over the body?
facilitatorNotes: “Hung” echoes the hanging. The star shows pity when the people do not, and it may be the star that “ever guided him,” yet could not save him. Nature mourns while the crowd celebrates.
evidence: All night a bright and solitary star
Hung pitifully o’er the swinging char.

questions.prompt: The last six lines turn to the crowd. What is most terrible about it, and what does “lynchers that were to be” predict?
facilitatorNotes: No woman shows sorrow, and the boys dance with glee: they are learning hatred and will become the next lynchers. The poem blames not only the mob but the whole watching community, and shows cruelty passed to children. “Steely blue” eyes mark the crowd as white.
evidence: The women thronged to look, but never a one Showed sorrow in her eyes of steely blue;
And little lads, lynchers that were to be, Danced round the dreadful thing in fiendish glee.
